clinicalPearls: Defined by chronic widespread musculoskeletal pain and tenderness, with pain present most of the day on most days for at least 3 months and distributed both above and below the waist, on both sides, and involving the axial skeleton (Harrison 22e p.2963).

Beyond pain, patients commonly report fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive dysfunction ("fibro fog"), anxiety, and depression, which may affect function and quality of life as much as or more than the pain itself (Harrison 22e p.2963-2964).

Elevated evoked pain sensitivity may be detected clinically by pain on blood-pressure cuff inflation or skin-roll tenderness; a formal tender-point exam applies ~4 kg/m2 of thumbnail pressure (enough to blanch the nail bed) at defined musculotendinous sites (Harrison 22e p.2963).

Older ACR criteria required 11 of 18 tender points; newer 2016 criteria abandon tender-point counting and instead use a Widespread Pain Index plus Symptom Severity Score (e.g., WPI >=7 and SSS >=5, or WPI 4-6 and SSS >=9, with generalized pain in at least 4 of 5 regions for >=3 months) (Harrison 22e p.2963-2964).
Tenderness is a continuous variable; strict application of a categorical threshold is not required for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2963).

Peripheral pain generators such as arthritis, bursitis, tendinitis, neuropathies, joint hypermobility, and scoliosis can trigger and perpetuate the centrally maintained widespread pain of FM (Harrison 22e p.2963).

FM is one of the chronic overlapping pain conditions and frequently coexists with myalgic encephalitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, temporomandibular disorder, chronic headaches, irritable bowel syndrome, and interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome, likely sharing central mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.2963).

The lifetime prevalence of mood disorders in FM approaches 80%; depression is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis, but screening for depressed mood and anhedonia is important (Harrison 22e p.2964).

Symptom onset and flares often cluster around periods of perceived stress, and there is a high prevalence of prior interpersonal or other violence exposure; consider posttraumatic stress disorder where relevant (Harrison 22e p.2964).
Some patients meeting FM criteria have a small-fiber neuropathy, and early reports suggest possible autoimmune changes in the peripheral nervous system in subsets of patients (Harrison 22e p.2964).

Functional assessment across physical, mental, and social domains is central, since improved function (rather than complete pain elimination) is the principal measure of management success (Harrison 22e p.2964).
harrison.pathophysiology: FM is regarded as a disorder in which the central nervous system maintains pain and the other core symptoms. Psychophysical testing shows altered afferent pain processing and impaired descending noxious inhibitory control, producing hyperalgesia and allodynia, and functional MRI demonstrates activation of pain-experiencing brain regions in response to stimuli that are innocuous in unaffected individuals. Pain perception is modulated by emotional and cognitive factors such as catastrophizing and perceived control. Genetic susceptibility appears polygenic, involving pathways that control pain and stress responses, including genes for metabolism, transport, and receptors of serotonin and other monoamines, with some genetic underpinnings shared across chronic pain conditions and overlapping with mood disorders. Peripheral pain generators (e.g., arthritis, bursitis, neuropathy, hypermobility) can serve as triggers that alter central pain processing (Harrison 22e p.2964).
additionalDifferentials: Connective tissue disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjogren's syndrome)
Multiple sclerosis and neuropathic pain syndromes
nonInfectiousMimics: Systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjogren's syndrome
Degenerative joint/spine/disk disease and myofascial pain syndromes
Neuropathic pain syndromes and multiple sclerosis
additionalInvestigations: Routine screen: ESR or CRP, complete blood count, and thyroid-stimulating hormone (results are normal in uncomplicated FM)
Guided by history/exam: complete metabolic panel, ANA, anti-SSA/anti-SSB, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, creatine phosphokinase
Viral (e.g., hepatitis C, HIV) and bacterial (e.g., Lyme) serologies when clinically indicated
Radiographs used sparingly and only when inflammatory arthritis is suspected; spine MRI reserved for features of inflammatory spine disease or neurologic symptoms
Repeat testing is discouraged unless the symptom complex changes
redFlags: Pain extending beyond what a known triggering or inflammatory condition could reasonably explain, signaling emergence of central FM-type pain requiring a different management focus
Objective inflammatory, neurologic, or systemic findings (abnormal ESR/CRP, focal neurologic deficits) that point toward an alternative or comorbid diagnosis rather than FM
Screen-positive major depression with anhedonia, and history suggestive of posttraumatic stress disorder, given high comorbidity and impact on outcome
harrison.prognosis: FM is a chronic condition with substantial adverse effects on physical and social functioning and on health-related quality of life. Outcomes are best when there is prompt diagnosis, assessment of pain, function, and psychosocial context, patient education, and a partnership-based strategy directed at improving function rather than eliminating pain; illness behaviors such as frequent physician visits are to be discouraged while function-promoting behaviors are encouraged (Harrison 22e p.2964-2965).
pitfalls: Failing to consider FM, leading to missed or delayed diagnosis since musculoskeletal pain is so common (Harrison 22e p.2964).
Over-investigating with repeated laboratory tests or, especially, spine MRI in the absence of inflammatory or neurologic features (Harrison 22e p.2964).
Continuing to treat only peripheral or inflammatory pain generators when central FM pain has emerged, instead of addressing central pain processing (Harrison 22e p.2964).
Setting complete pain elimination, rather than improved function and quality of life, as the treatment goal (Harrison 22e p.2965).
harrison.severityClassification: Severity is captured by the 2016 diagnostic instrument combining the Widespread Pain Index (WPI, range 0-19) and the Symptom Severity Score (SSS, range 0-12, grading fatigue, unrefreshing waking, and cognitive symptoms plus selected somatic items). Diagnosis requires WPI >=7 and SSS >=5, or WPI 4-6 and SSS >=9, with generalized pain in at least 4 of 5 body regions, sustained for at least 3 months; higher WPI and SSS values reflect greater symptom burden (Harrison 22e p.2964).
management: Ground care in patient education and a partnership-based, self-management approach
Prescribe graded aerobic and strengthening exercise as the core non-pharmacological intervention
Offer cognitive behavioural therapy and address sleep, mood and psychosocial contributors

Use centrally acting pharmacotherapy such as tricyclic agents like amitriptyline, serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors like duloxetine, or gabapentinoids like pregabalin, while avoiding opioids
Identify and treat peripheral pain generators and comorbid conditions that perpetuate central sensitisation
Coordinate multidisciplinary, multimodal care across physiotherapy, psychology and primary care
Review pain, function and quality of life regularly, adjusting the plan and avoiding unnecessary repeat investigations
